Charmer
CHARM-er
noun
From the Latin carmen, “a song, an incantation,” through Old French charme. A charm was first a chanted formula meant to bind or command; only later did the word soften into a trinket or a pleasing manner.

Biblical Definition

In the KJV a charmer is not a pleasant companion but a caster of spells. The word comes from the Latin carmen, “a song” or “incantation”: a charm was first a chanted formula meant to bind, heal, curse, or command by the mere power of uttered words. The modern reader, who calls a gracious man “charming” and a bracelet a “charm,” must strip the word back to its old and sinister sense. The law forbids him outright, setting the charmer among the diviners no Israelite might harbour. The Psalmist reaches for the serpent-charmer to picture the hardened sinner, the deaf adder “which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely” (Psa 58:5) — the wicked are more deaf to God than a snake to the most skilful spell. When Isaiah foretells Egypt’s collapse, he shows her turning in terror to every occult prop: “they shall seek to the idols, and to the charmers, and to them that have familiar spirits, and to the wizards” (Isa 19:3) — and none of them can lift the judgment the LORD has spoken. Solomon’s proverb mocks the whole art with a shrug: “Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment” (Ecc 10:11). The charm is a chant, and the chant is a lie. The LORD alone speaks words that truly bind and loose, and He forbids His people to seek any other tongue for their safety or their fate.

Webster 1828 Definition

One who works enchantment by chanted spells — from carmen, a song or incantation, not a mere pleasing manner.

CHARMER, one that uses or has power of charms or enchantments; one who binds by spell or incantation.

From Latin carmen, “a song, an incantation,” through Old French charme.

The AV sense is the serpent-charmer and the spell-caster, not the modern “charming” personality.

The deaf adder will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely (Psa 58:5).

Egypt in her ruin sought to the charmers and the wizards, and found no help (Isa 19:3).

Key Scripture

Psa 58:5 — "Which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely."

Isa 19:3 — "And the spirit of Egypt shall fail in the midst thereof; and I will destroy the counsel thereof: and they shall seek to the idols, and to the charmers, and to them that have familiar spirits, and to the wizards."

Ecc 10:11 — "Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment; and a babbler is no better."

Deu 18:12 — "For all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD: and because of these abominations the LORD thy God doth drive them out from before thee."

Modern Corruption

Two shifts meet here: the innocent drift by which “charming” came to mean merely delightful, and the live revival of literal spell-craft — love-spells, “spell jars,” and word-magic — that is the AV’s charmer come again.

expand to see more

The honest drift is easy to name: from a chanted spell (carmen) the word softened to a locket on a bracelet, and then to a pleasant manner, so that we call a winsome man charming and mean no witchcraft at all. But under that softening the old thing has resurfaced with a vengeance. The neo-pagan revival peddles literal charms: the love-spell to bind another’s will, the “spell jar” buried by the door, the whispered affirmation that claims to bend reality by the power of the spoken word. This is carmen exactly — binding by incantation — and the AV forbids it as an abomination, whatever gentle name it now wears.

Scripture answers the charm with the word of God, the only utterance that truly binds and looses. The law that names a charmer among the forbidden also declares that “all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD” (Deu 18:12), and Isaiah recalls the seeker to the sufficient testimony: “to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). The believer needs no spell to secure love, safety, or tomorrow; he has a Father who hears prayer and a Christ whose bare word stilled the sea. To reach for a charm is to distrust that word and to court the very powers Christ came to destroy. The serpent bites without enchantment, and the charmer perishes with his song.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word is carmen, “a song, incantation” — a caster of spells, not a delightful companion.

Charmer — from Latin carmen, “a song, an incantation.”

A charm was first a chanted formula to bind or command, kin to the enchanter’s art.

The serpent-charmer stands behind the imagery of the deaf adder (Psa 58:5).

Egypt in her fall sought the charmers among her idols and wizards (Isa 19:3).

The modern “charming” personality is a softened ghost of the old, sinister sense.

Usage

"The AV charmer is a spell-caster, not a delightful guest — the deaf adder ignores his charming."

"A charm in Scripture is a carmen, a chanted incantation, forbidden to every son of Israel."

"Egypt, judged of God, ran to the charmers — and the serpent bit her anyway, without enchantment."
